Deep eutectic solvent-mediated demethylation of citrus polymethoxyflavones: Effects, optimization, and bioactivity evaluation
Zimao Ye a,¹ , Shunjie Li c,¹ , Juan Juan Wei e , Yurong Li a , Zhiqin Zhou a,b,d,*

ABSTRACT

Deep eutectic solvent (DES)-mediated demethylation presents a novel strategy for valorizing agricultural waste. This study investigated the demethylation of polymethoxyflavones (PMFs) from citrus peel with DES and its effects on final products' biological activity. Six DESs with different functional groups (carboxylic acid, alcohol and amide) were compared for PMF demethylation efficiency. Results showed that acidic DES effectively promoted PMF demethylation to form 5-hydroxy-polymethoxyflavones (5-OH-PMFs), with pH, hydrogen bond strength, polarity and reaction temperature being key factors. Under optimized conditions (1:5 g/L solid-liquid ratio, 480 W microwave power, 10 min), choline chloride/citric acid achieved 96.32 ± 0.06% demethylation efficiency. Moreover, the system retained a conversion efficiency above 75% after four consecutive cycles. Bioactivity evaluation further revealed that 5-OH-PMFs exhibited significantly enhanced antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects compared to PMFs in RAW264.7 cells, due to increased antioxidant enzyme activity and elevated expression of anti-inflammatory factors. Simulated gastrointestinal digestion further improved 5-OH-PMF bioavailability. In summary, this study demonstrated the effectiveness of using DES to catalyze PMFs demethylation as a promising and sustainable method to enhance their bioactivity. It provides a new perspective for preparing demethylated bioactive compounds from citrus and other plant resources.

1. Introduction Deep eutectic solvents (DES) are a class of novel green solvents that have garnered significant attention (Mavai et al., 2025). In recent years, DES have been widely used as novel green solvents for extracting bioactive compounds from various plant resources (Huang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025). Notably, DES not only efficiently extracts target

compounds but also simultaneously catalyzes molecular structural transformations (Chen et al., 2023). Currently, the application of DES in the conversion of bioactive substances is primarily focused on deglycosylation reactions. Sun et al. (2020) utilized a one-pot method based on DES to extract polygonum glycosides from polygonum and simultaneously convert them into resveratrol, a process involving the cleavage of glycosidic bonds. Similarly, multiple studies have confirmed the su- perior performance of DES in promoting the deglycosylation reactions of glycoside compounds such as soybean isoflavone glycosides (Chen et al., 2023). These studies utilize the acidic environment and hydrogen bond network structure of DES to promote the hydrolysis and cleavage of glycosidic bonds, thereby achieving the conversion of glycoside com- pounds into aglycones. However, the potential application of DES in other types of bioactive substance conversion reactions remains largely unexplored.

Demethylation modification plays an important role in enhancing the biological activity of natural products. Recent studies have revealed the potential of DES to promote demethylation reactions during ligno-cellulose processing. For instance, studies indicate that during the stepwise separation and depolymerisation of lignin by acidic DES, the demethylation of lignin structural units occurs concurrently with the cleavage of β-O-4' ether bonds (Hong et al., 2020). However, thoses studies mainly focus on the overall conversion of biopolymeric macro-molecules such as lignin, with no systematic investigation into deme-thylation reactions within specific bioactive compounds (Hong et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2025). It is unclear whether DESs can serve as efficient green catalysts for the selective demethylation of small-molecule bioactive substances. Inspired by the demethylation phenomena observed in lignin studies, we hypothesise that DES may offer an inno-vative and effective strategy for the controlled demethylation of bioac-tive molecules.

Polymethoxyflavones (PMFs) are characteristic secondary metabo- lites produced by citrus plants, exhibiting bioactivities such as antioxi- dant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer, and lipid metabolism regulation (Peng et al., 2022). However, the primary active forms of PMFs that exert their effects in vivo are their demethylated products. These demethylated PMFs exhibit significantly enhanced bioavailability compared to their original forms (Ho et al., 2020). This makes the demethylation of PMFs a key pathway for enhancing the functional value of citrus resources. Several studies have explored various ap- proaches to convert PMFs to 5-OH-PMFs, including acid hydrolysis (Li et al., 2007), thermal treatment (Zhang et al., 2019a, 2019b) and mi- crobial biotransformation (Łużny et al., 2021). Among these, Brønsted acid-based hydrolysis has emerged as the main method for producing 5-OH-PMFs (Huang et al., 2019). The reaction mechanism likely due to the following: (1) existence of lone pairs of oxygen atoms in the methoxy group of PMFs and the oxygen atom of the adjacent carbonyl group, which are prone to proton activation; (2) presence of acidic solution providing protons; (3) the proton hydrogen and electron donating ox- ygen coordination to form a stable six-membered ring structure; (4) the broken covalent bond between the oxygen atom and methyl group; (5) hydrolysis of the six-membered ring to form a hydroxyl group (Huang et al., 2019). However, liquid acids are difficult to recover, corrode equipment, and pollute the environment. Although heating is safer, it is inefficient and offers low product selectivity. Microbial conversion re- quires complex equipment and similarly exhibits poor selectivity. These limitations hinder the realization of green production goals.

Various physical techniques are also extensively used to enhance demethylation. High-temperature treatment significantly increases re- action rates. For instance, phosphoric acid-catalysed demethylation of naringin achieves 93.71% conversion within two hours at 175 °C (Huang et al., 2019). Hot pressurised water technology enhances acid-catalysed demethylation by altering water's physicochemical properties (Bocus et al., 2025). Ultrasound-assisted technology (UAE) uses locally generated high temperatures and pressures via cavitation effects to disrupt plant cell walls and enhance mass transfer (Sun et al., 2020). Microwave-assisted technology (MAE) selectively heats polar molecules, inducing intense molecular motion and friction to accelerate chemical reactions (Zhang et al., 2025). These studies demonstrate that integrating physical enhancement techniques with DES holds
considerable potential, offering diverse intensification approaches for PMF demethylation.

This study investigated the effects of DES type (carboxylic acid, alcohol and amide-based), physicochemical properties (pH, hydrogen bond strength, Kamlet-Taft parameter), and physical techniques (mi- crowave, high temperature and pressure, ultrasound-bath) on the demethylation of PMFs. Based on this, key reaction parameters were optimized, including microwave power, reaction time, DES water con- tent, and feed-to-liquid ratio. Additionally, the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities of 5-OH-PMFs were evaluated. The results of this study indicate that acidic DES have potential in the preparation of hy- droxylated PMFs extracts and other demethylated bioactive compounds.

## 2. Methods ### 2.1. Chemicals Choline chloride (ChCl, ≥ 98%), oxalic acid (OA, ≥ 98%), citric acid (CA, ≥ 99%), lactic acid (LA, ≥ 99 %), Glycerine (Gly, ≥ 98%), 1,4-Butanediol (BDO, ≥ 99%), urea (UA, ≥ 99%) and acetic acid (≥ 98%) were purchased from Macklin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). Standards included isosinensetin (ISO), sinensetin (SIN), nobiletin (NOB), tangeretin (TAN), 5-Demethylnobiletin (5-DN) and 5-Demethyltangeretin (5-DT), all sourced from Yuanye Bio-Technology Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China). Sigma Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA) provided Folin-Ciocalteu reagent, acetonitrile, Petroleum ether, methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), 2,2'-azinobis 3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid (ABTS), 1,1-diphenyl-2-picrylhydrazyl radical (DPPH), 2,4,6-tripyridyl-s-triazine (TPTZ). Lipopolysaccharides (LPS) were purchased from Nanjing Herbal Bio-technology Co., Ltd (Nanjing, China). Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) was purchased from Chongqing Chuandong Chemical Co., Ltd (Chongqing, China). Pepsin, Trypsin, Pancreatic lipase and bile salts were purchased from Macklin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd (Shanghai, China).

## 2.2. Materials Mature citrus fruits (_Citrus reticulata_ Blanco cv. 'Nanfeng tangerine') were collected from the National Citrus Germplasm Repository (Chongqing, China). Healthy fruits of average size at maturity were harvested from 5 trees per variety. The peel was peeled and rinsed with water and then air-dried at 50 °C. The dried samples were ground into powder and filtered through a 60-mesh sieve. The powder obtained was stored in a dry and light-proof environment until use.

RAW264.7 mouse macrophages and specific culture medium were purchased from Wuhan ProCells Biomedical Technology Co., Ltd. (Wuhan, China). Malondialdehyde kit, glutathione kit, superoxide dismutase kit, catalase kit, and glutathione reductase kit were purchased from Beijing Solarbio Science & Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). RNA extraction kit, RNA reverse transcription, and quantitative kits were purchased from Beijing TIANGEN Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China).

2.3. PMF extraction and analysis PMFs were extracted from citrus peels following the method previously described by Zheng et al. (2022). In brief, petroleum ether is used to extract crude PMFs, which are then washed with MTBE to obtain PMFs extracts. The extracts are stored in dry, dark bottles for subsequent use. The identification and quantification of PMFs were conducted according to the method described by Chen et al. (2022). Briefly, chromatographic analysis was performed on a Waters HPLC instrument equipped with a photodiode array (PDA) detector (Milford, MA, USA) and a SunFire C18 chromatographic column (4.6 × 250 mm, 5µm, USA). The column temperature was set at 40 °C. 0.01 % acetic acid and acetonitrile were used as mobile phases A and B. The flow rate was set at

The final converted products were detected using a non-targeted metabolomics approach, with the procedure strictly adhering to our previous research methodology (Ye et al., 2025).

## 2.4. DES preparation and characterization ChCl was utilized as a general HBA, while carboxylic acids—OA, CA, and LA—alcohols such as Gly and BDO, and the UA were employed as HBDs. These were mixed with the HBA at various molar ratios. The preparation of all DES was carried out by heating, following the method outlined by Abbott et al. (2004). Relevant details regarding the compositions are summarized in supplementary Table S2.

The chemical functional groups of DES were characterized using Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FT-IR) (Shimadzu IRTracer-100, Japan) in ATR mode, covering a scanning range from 400 to 4000 cm⁻¹. Thermogravimetric analysis (TG) was performed using an SDT 650 thermoanalyser (TA Instruments). Thermograms were recorded in a nitrogen atmosphere with a heating rate of 10 °C/min from 30 to 600 °C. ¹H NMR spectra were recorded on a JNM-ECZ600R spectrometer. Samples were dissolved in deuterium oxide (D₂O) prior to analysis. Each spectrum was acquired with 1024 scans and a relaxation delay of 2 s. The viscosity of DES was measured using a MCR92 rotational rheometer (Anton Paar, Austria). The lower plate temperature was regulated by a conical plate temperature control system and steady shear viscosity measurements were performed at 25 °C and 150 °C with a shear rate of 50 s⁻¹. The pH of DES was determined using a pH meter (PHSJ-5, INESA, China). For solvent color development parameters (π*, β and α) of DES, N,N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline, 4-nitroaniline, and Nile red were used as dye indicators for determination, respectively. The parameters for solvent color development were calculated according to Zhang et al. (2023).

2.5. PMF Processing with DES To evaluate the conversion rate and feasibility of DES in the trans- formation of PMFs into 5-OH-PMFs, this study selected different types of DES (carboxylic acid, alcohol and amide-based) and assessed their conversion performance under various conditions, including ultrasonic bath, microwave, and high-temperature and pressure treatments. Sub- sequently, Comprehensive optimization experiment was conducted to investigate the main parameters influencing the conversion process. The parameters examined included power levels of 160, 320, 480, 640 and 800 W; material-to-liquid ratios (g/L) of 1:5, 1:2, 1:1, 2:1, and 5:1; re- action times of 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 min; and DES water contents (%) of 0, 5, 10, 15, and 20.

Following the conversion reaction, the DES solution was mixed with an equal volume of ultrapure water and stored at 4 °C for 24 h. The solution was then centrifuged to collect the precipitate. The analysis of 5-OH-PMFs was performed using the method described in 2.3. The conversion efficiency (CE) of PMFs into 5-OH-PMFs was calculated using the following formula:
Conversion efficiency(CE%) = $\frac{C_{ahp} - C_{ohp}}{C_{op}} \times \frac{M_{wp}}{M_{whp}} \times 100\%$

where C$_{op}$ and C$_{ohp}$ represent the original contents of PMFs and 5-OH-PMFs in the extract (mg/g), C$_{ahp}$ represents the content of 5-OH-PMFs in the product after the reaction (mg/g), M$_{wp}$ and and M$_{whp}$ denote the molecular weights of the respective substances (g/mol). The CE was ultimately calculated based on the actual substances participating in the conversion process.

### 2.6. Recovery of DESs The DES recycling process was informed by the methodology described in the previous study (Wen et al., 2024). Briefly, an equal volume of water was added to the used DES solution, and the mixture was centrifuged to collect the supernatant. The collected supernatant was then transferred to a rotary evaporator to remove water, enabling the recovery of the DES solution for reuse.

2.7. _Biological activity assessment_ 2.7.1. _Chemical Antioxidant Activity_ The chemical antioxidant capacity of the samples was evaluated using ABTS, DPPH, and FRAP assays, following the method described by Wang et al. (2025). The results were expressed as µmol Trolox equivalent (TE) per gram of extract, a standard unit for assessing antioxidant activity.

2.7.2. Cellular antioxidant activity The cytotoxicity of PMFs and 5-OH-PMFs was evaluated using the CCK-8 assay in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions to screen for the optimal dosage. An oxidative stress model was then established by treating cultured cells with 0.03% H2O2. PMFs and 5-OH-PMFs were first dissolved in DMSO and subsequently diluted to a fixed concentration using complete culture medium. After 20 h of treatment, cell samples were collected for further biochemical analysis. The anti-oxidant capacity of the extracts was assessed using oxidative stress markers, including malondialdehyde (MDA), glutathione (GSH), superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), and glutathione reductase (GR). All assays were performed in strict accordance with the manufacturer's protocols.

### 2.7.3. Cell anti-inflammatory activity RAW264.7 cells were seeded into 6-well plates at an initial density of 3 x 10⁵ cells per well and cultured for 24 h at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 incubator. The cells were then pretreated with PMFs, 5-OH-PMFs, or DMSO for 24 h. Subsequently, fresh culture medium containing 3 µg/mL LPS or without LPS was added, and the cells were incubated for an additional 4 h. Following incubation, the cells were collected to measure nitric oxide (NO) levels and to analyze the mRNA expression levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α, IL-1β) and anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10, TGF-β). RNA extraction and reverse transcription were performed according to the manufacturer's instructions. Quantitative analysis was carried out using the SYBR Green ProTaq HS Premix qPCR kit (Vazyme, Nanjing, China). Gene-specific primers were synthesized by UW Genetics (Shenzhen, China) and are listed in Supplementary Table S3.

2.7.4. In vitro digestion The in vitro digestion process was conducted following the protocol outlined by Brodkorb et al. (2019). The digestion buffers for the simulated oral phase (1.25 ×SSF), gastric phase (1.25 ×SGF), and intestinal phase (1.25 ×SIF) consisted of KCl, KH2PO4, NaHCO3, NaCl, MgCl2, (NH4)CO3, CaCl2, HCl, and ddH2O. Simulated saliva (SSF) was prepared using 1.25 ×SSF and ddH2O. Simulated gastric fluid (SGF) included 1.25 SGF, pepsin, HCl, and ddH2O, while simulated intestinal fluid (SIF) comprised 1.25 ×SIF, Trypsin, Pancreatic lipase, bile salts, NaOH, and ddH2O. 1 M HCl and 1 M NaOH are used to adjust the pH of the

digestion solution, with the volumes recorded. Prior to digestion, 40 mg of 5-OH-PMFs and PMFs were suspended in 5 mL of PBS. During the oral digestion phase, 5 mL of the suspension was mixed with 5 mL of SSF at a 1:1 (v/v) ratio and incubated at pH 7.0, 37 °C, and 100 rpm for 2 min. Subsequently, an equal volume of SGF was added to the mixture, followed by incubation at pH 3.0, 37 °C, and 100 rpm for 2 h to simulate gastric digestion. Finally, an equal volume of SIF was introduced to the digestion solution, and the mixture was incubated at pH 7.0, 37 °C, and 100 rpm for an additional 2 h to simulate intestinal digestion. After each digestion phase, 2 mL of the digestion solution containing terminal samples was collected, centri- fuged at 3000 ×g for 10 min to obtain the supernatant, and filtered through a 0.22 µm membrane. The filtered supernatants were then analyzed using HPLC to quantify the content of 5-OH-PMFs (5-DN/5- DT) and PMFs (NOB/TAN). Solubility for each digestion phase was calculated based on the HPLC results.
2.8. _Data statistical analysis_ Data are expressed as mean \u00b1 standard deviation and repeated at least 3 times. One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and Duncan's test
were performed using SPSS 20.0 software, with a significance level set at p < 0.05 to assess statistical significance. R was used for correlation analysis.

### 3. Results and Discussion #### 3.1. Preparation and characterization of citrus PMFs and synthetic DES ##### 3.1.1. Enrichment and analysis of PMFs from citrus A high-purity mixture of PMFs from citrus peels was prepared according to the strategy illustrated in Fig. 1A. A two-step method was utilized for the selective isolation of the target PMFs compounds. The crude extract was first obtained by reflux extraction using petroleum ether. This solvent was chosen due to prior research that identified it as the most effective for extracting PMFs from citrus peel (Zheng et al., 2022). However, as crude PMFs extract typically contain lipid-soluble impurities such as essential oils and carotenoids (Mahato et al., 2019). Consequently, subsequent purification by washing with MTBE effectively removed residual impurities (Matyash et al., 2008).
The purified PMFs extract was then subjected to qualitative and quantitative analysis using UPLC-QqQ-MS/MS and HPLC-DAD,

### 3.3.3. Effect of Microwave Power As shown in Fig. 5C, the conversion efficiency follows a trend of initially increasing and then decreasing with changes in microwave power. At 160 W, the conversion efficiency reaches its minimum value (80.01 ± 0.88 %). Increasing the power to 480 W results in the highest conversion efficiency (90.47 ± 0.74 %, p < 0.05). However, further increasing the power to 800 W results in a significant decrease in conversion efficiency, dropping to 84.37 % (p < 0.05). This decline is likely attributable to the degradation of PMFs under excessive microwave power. High microwave power can generate intense localized 'hot spots' within the reaction system, leading to rapid and potentially uncontrolled temperature increases. Flavonoids, including PMFs, are known to be thermally sensitive (Huang et al., 2019). Therefore, while a certain level of microwave power is necessary to overcome the activation energy for the demethylation reaction, excessive power appears to be detrimental, causing compound degradation that outweighs the increase in conversion rate. Based on these findings, this experiment determined 480 W as the optimal microwave power, as it balances maximizing conversion efficiency with minimizing the risk of molecular degradation.

3.3.4. *Effect of Processing Time* Reaction time is a key parameter affecting conversion efficiency. The results indicate that extending the reaction time significantly affects conversion efficiency (Fig. 5D). At a reaction time of 2 min, the conversion efficiency was the lowest (88.85 ± 0.05%). As reaction time increases, conversion efficiency gradually improves and reaches its maximum value at 10 min (96.32 ± 0.06%, p < 0.05). Considering both conversion efficiency and cost-effectiveness, 10 min was determined to be the optimal reaction time.

Based on this, the optimal process parameters for the DES2 system to efficiently catalyze the hydroxylation of PMFs were determined as follows: a solid-to-liquid ratio of 1:5 (g/L), microwave power of 480 W, and a reaction time of 10 min. The results confirmed that 5-DN and 5-DT were the most predominant 5-OH-PMFs. While trace amounts of other potential molecular were detected, their relative abundance was significantly lower than that of 5-DN and 5-DT (Supplementary Table S9). Therefore, subsequent quantitative analysis and mechanistic studies were focused on these two major compounds.

3.5. Comparison with other methods To date, various methods have been developed to hydroxylate PMFs into 5-OH-PMFs (Table 2). This study presents a novel microwave-assisted conversion system based on a deep eutectic solvent composed of choline chloride and citric acid (ChCl/CA). By optimizing process parameters, this method achieves significantly enhanced conversion efficiency. Compared with existing methods, this approach offers notable advantages, including environmental sustainability, high efficiency, and operational simplicity.

Traditional conversion methods employing boron tribromide (BBr3) achieve high conversion efficiency but require toxic reagents and must be conducted under stringent conditions, such as low temperatures and the use of high-purity solvents. Additionally, these methods generate substantial quantities of hazardous byproducts during post-reaction processing, posing environmental and safety concerns (Li et al., 2007). The conversion method based on heating with hydrochloric acid, while requiring less specialized equipment, involves a prolonged reaction time of up to 24 h. Moreover, the corrosive and volatile nature of hydro- chloric acid creates operational safety risks, which limit its feasibility for industrial applications (XU et al., 2015). In recent years, edible acid-phosphoric acid systems have gained attention due to their higher safety profile. However, such systems require a reaction time of 2 h and achieve a conversion rate of approximately 93%, leaving room for improvement in both efficiency and product purification (Huang et al., 2019). The ChCl/CA DES system proposed in this study addresses many of the limitations associated with traditional methods. It eliminates the need for toxic reagents, significantly reduces reaction time, and operates under milder and safer conditions. Despite the absence of detailed economic cost-benefit analysis, the observed advantages in terms of higher yield, reduced processing time, and the use of greener, recyclable solvents suggest that the DES-based method holds significant potential

Specifically, 5-OH-PMFs significantly reduced MDA levels and enhanced the activity of SOD, CAT, GR, and GSH, bringing their levels comparable to those of the control group (p < 0.05) (Fig. 7C). The superior antioxidant activity of 5-OH-PMFs can be attributed to the structural modification of a hydroxyl group at the C5-position (Lai et al., 2015). The fundamental mechanism for radical scavenging by flavonoids involves the donation of a hydrogen atom from a hydroxyl group to neutralize a free radical (Lai et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018). Specifically, the hydroxyl group at the C5-position plays a pivotal role. 5-OH group forms a strong intramolecular hydrogen bond with the adjacent carbonyl oxygen at the C4-position (Li et al., 2006). This intramolecular hydrogen bond not only stabilizes the parent molecule but, more importantly, stabilizes the phenoxyl radical formed after hydrogen donation. This stabilization effect lowers the bond dissociation energy of the 5-OH group, making it a more efficient hydrogen donor and thus enhancing the molecule's overall ability to scavenge free radicals and terminate oxidative chain reactions. These findings highlight the potential of 5-OH-PMFs as potent antioxidants, offering promising applications in functional foods or as therapeutic agents for oxidative stress-related diseases.

### 3.6.2. Anti-inflammatory activity of 5-OH-PMFs The anti-inflammatory activity of PMFs and 5-OH-PMFs were evaluated in a LPS-induced inflammatory model in RAW264.7 cells. As shown in Fig. 7D, both PMFs and 5-OH-PMFs inhibited nitric oxide (NO) production in a concentration-dependent manner. Notably, 5-OH-PMFs exhibited significantly higher efficacy, reducing NO levels were reduced to near baseline levels at a concentration of 20 µg/mL. In terms of cytokine regulation, 5-OH-PMFs exhibited superior activity compared to PMFs. Specifically, 5-OH-PMFs significantly upregulated the expression of anti-inflammatory cytokines (such as TGF-β and IL-10) while effectively suppressing the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α). These results highlight the potential of 5-OH-PMFs as a more potent anti-inflammatory agent than PMFs. Their ability to regulate inflammatory mediators and restore cytokine balance makes them a promising candidate for therapeutic strategies in the management of inflammatory diseases.

3.6.3. In vitro digestion of 5-OH-PMFs A three-stage in vitro digestion model (oral-gastric-intestinal) was employed to investigate the solubility changes of 5-OH-PMFs and PMFs throughout different stages of digestion. As depicted in Fig. 7E, the solubility of all tested compounds increased to varying extents following simulated gastrointestinal digestion. Among the three stages, intestinal digestion exerted the most pronounced solubilization effect, followed by gastric digestion, while oral digestion had a comparatively minor impact. Specifically, the solubility of 5-DN prior to digestion was 1.27 ± 0.09%, which increased to 1.67 ± 0.02% after oral digestion, further rose to 2.99 ± 0.007% after gastric digestion, and significantly surged to 13.04 ± 0.16% following intestinal digestion. Conversely, the solu- bility of NOB during the respective digestion stages was 1.78 ± 0.04%, 1.89 ± 0.005%, 2.82 ± 0.01%, and 4.35 ± 0.05%. Remarkably, the solubility of 5-DN post-intestinal digestion was approximately three times greater than that of NOB (p < 0.05). Interestingly, the solubility of TAN was significantly higher than that of 5-DT across all stages of digestion (p < 0.05), which contrasted the trend observed in the 5-DN/ NOB comparison. These findings indicate that the influence of hydroxy substitution on solubility behavior is compound-specific.

The findings demonstrate that the intestinal environment exerts the most pronounced promotive effect on the solubility of flavonoids, aligning with the established understanding that flavonoids are pre- dominantly absorbed in the intestine (Karn et al., 2021). The substantial increase in solubility observed during the intestinal digestion phase can likely be attributed to the solubilizing action of bile salts. These salts

exhibit surfactant properties that facilitate the formation of micellar structures with hydrophobic flavonoids, thereby markedly enhancing their solubility in aqueous systems(Obeid et al., 2025). Furthermore, the distinct solubility profiles of 5-OH-PMFs and PMFs throughout digestion underscore the critical role of molecular structure in determining bioavailability. Typically, the hydroxyl group serves as a hydrogen bond donor, which strengthens interactions with polar solvents, thus potentially increasing solubility (Lee et al., 2023). However, 5-DT exhibits lower solubility compared to TAN, which may be attributed to its higher log P value (Supplementary Table S10). This increased lipophilicity is likely a result of hydrogen bonding interactions between the 5-hydroxy group and the adjacent carbonyl atom (Zhang et al., 2021). Elevated lipophilicity generally enhances a compound's intestinal membrane permeability, potentially contributing to increased biological activity in vivo.

4. Conclusion This study demonstrated that employing strong carboxylic acid-based DES for the demethylation modification of citrus PMFs represents a green and sustainable strategy for enhancing the biological activity of PMFs. The pH, hydrogen bond strength, Kamlet-Taft α, and π* parameters of DES were identified as the key factors influencing PMF demethylation. Based on this, a green method was developed using a microwave-assisted choline chloride-citric acid (ChCl/CA) deep eutectic solvent system to catalyze citrus PMFs for the production of 5-OH-PMFs (primarily 5-DN and 5-DT). The optimal conversion efficiency of PMFs under this system reached 96.32 ± 0.06%. Compared with traditional methods, this system significantly shortened the reaction time, demonstrating higher reaction efficiency and resource utilization. Additionally, 5-OH-PMFs exhibited markedly enhanced antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities compared to their parent compounds, highlighting their potential applications in health-related products. However, the high viscosity of the DES system presents a challenge for operational simplicity. Fortunately, this limitation can potentially be mitigated through further optimization of the DES formulation. Additionally, the transformative mechanism of DES in the hydroxylation of PMFs warrants further investigation, which could provide valuable theoretical insights for designing customized DES formulations tailored to the preparation of natural bioactive compounds. In summary, this study provides a promising technical approach for the efficient preparation of 5-OH-PMFs and lays a solid foundation for their future development and application in bioactive product innovation.

Similarly, multiple studies have confirmed the su- perior performance of DES in promoting the deglycosylation reactions of glycoside compounds such as soybean isoflavone glycosides (Chen et al., 2023). These studies utilize the acidic environment and hydrogen bond network structure of DES to promote the hydrolysis and cleavage of glycosidic bonds, thereby achieving the conversion of glycoside com- pounds into aglycones. However, the potential application of DES in other types of bioactive substance conversion reactions remains largely unexplored. Demethylation modification plays an important role in enhancing the biological activity of natural products. Recent studies have revealed the potential of DES to promote demethylation reactions during ligno-cellulose processing. For instance, studies indicate that during the stepwise separation and depolymerisation of lignin by acidic DES, the demethylation of lignin structural units occurs concurrently with the cleavage of β-O-4' ether bonds (Hong et al., 2020). However, thoses studies mainly focus on the overall conversion of biopolymeric macro-molecules such as lignin, with no systematic investigation into deme-thylation reactions within specific bioactive compounds (Hong et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2025). It is unclear whether DESs can serve as efficient green catalysts for the selective demethylation of small-molecule bioactive substances. Inspired by the demethylation phenomena observed in lignin studies, we hypothesise that DES may offer an inno-vative and effective strategy for the controlled demethylation of bioac-tive molecules. Polymethoxyflavones (PMFs) are characteristic secondary metabo- lites produced by citrus plants, exhibiting bioactivities such as antioxi- dant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer, and lipid metabolism regulation (Peng et al., 2022). However, the primary active forms of PMFs that exert their effects in vivo are their demethylated products. These demethylated PMFs exhibit significantly enhanced bioavailability compared to their original forms (Ho et al., 2020). This makes the demethylation of PMFs a key pathway for enhancing the functional value of citrus resources. Several studies have explored various ap- proaches to convert PMFs to 5-OH-PMFs, including acid hydrolysis (Li et al., 2007), thermal treatment (Zhang et al., 2019a, 2019b) and mi- crobial biotransformation (Łużny et al., 2021). Among these, Brønsted acid-based hydrolysis has emerged as the main method for producing 5-OH-PMFs (Huang et al., 2019). The reaction mechanism likely due to the following: (1) existence of lone pairs of oxygen atoms in the methoxy group of PMFs and the oxygen atom of the adjacent carbonyl group, which are prone to proton activation; (2) presence of acidic solution providing protons; (3) the proton hydrogen and electron donating ox- ygen coordination to form a stable six-membered ring structure; (4) the broken covalent bond between the oxygen atom and methyl group; (5) hydrolysis of the six-membered ring to form a hydroxyl group (Huang et al., 2019). However, liquid acids are difficult to recover, corrode equipment, and pollute the environment. Although heating is safer, it is inefficient and offers low product selectivity. Microbial conversion re- quires complex equipment and similarly exhibits poor selectivity. These limitations hinder the realization of green production goals. Various physical techniques are also extensively used to enhance demethylation. High-temperature treatment significantly increases re- action rates. For instance, phosphoric acid-catalysed demethylation of naringin achieves 93.71% conversion within two hours at 175 °C (Huang et al., 2019). Hot pressurised water technology enhances acid-catalysed demethylation by altering water's physicochemical properties (Bocus et al., 2025). Ultrasound-assisted technology (UAE) uses locally generated high temperatures and pressures via cavitation effects to disrupt plant cell walls and enhance mass transfer (Sun et al., 2020). Microwave-assisted technology (MAE) selectively heats polar molecules, inducing intense molecular motion and friction to accelerate chemical reactions (Zhang et al., 2025). These studies demonstrate that integrating physical enhancement techniques with DES holds considerable potential, offering diverse intensification approaches for PMF demethylation. This study investigated the effects of DES type (carboxylic acid, alcohol and amide-based), physicochemical properties (pH, hydrogen bond strength, Kamlet-Taft parameter), and physical techniques (mi- crowave, high temperature and pressure, ultrasound-bath) on the demethylation of PMFs. Based on this, key reaction parameters were optimized, including microwave power, reaction time, DES water con- tent, and feed-to-liquid ratio. Additionally, the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities of 5-OH-PMFs were evaluated. The results of this study indicate that acidic DES have potential in the preparation of hy- droxylated PMFs extracts and other demethylated bioactive compounds. ## 2. Methods ### 2.1. PMF Processing with DES To evaluate the conversion rate and feasibility of DES in the trans- formation of PMFs into 5-OH-PMFs, this study selected different types of DES (carboxylic acid, alcohol and amide-based) and assessed their conversion performance under various conditions, including ultrasonic bath, microwave, and high-temperature and pressure treatments. Sub- sequently, Comprehensive optimization experiment was conducted to investigate the main parameters influencing the conversion process. The parameters examined included power levels of 160, 320, 480, 640 and 800 W; material-to-liquid ratios (g/L) of 1:5, 1:2, 1:1, 2:1, and 5:1; re- action times of 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 min; and DES water contents (%) of 0, 5, 10, 15, and 20. Following the conversion reaction, the DES solution was mixed with an equal volume of ultrapure water and stored at 4 °C for 24 h. The solution was then centrifuged to collect the precipitate. The analysis of 5-OH-PMFs was performed using the method described in 2.3. The conversion efficiency (CE) of PMFs into 5-OH-PMFs was calculated using the following formula: Conversion efficiency(CE%) = $\frac{C_{ahp} - C_{ohp}}{C_{op}} \times \frac{M_{wp}}{M_{whp}} \times 100\%$ where C$_{op}$ and C$_{ohp}$ represent the original contents of PMFs and 5-OH-PMFs in the extract (mg/g), C$_{ahp}$ represents the content of 5-OH-PMFs in the product after the reaction (mg/g), M$_{wp}$ and and M$_{whp}$ denote the molecular weights of the respective substances (g/mol). The CE was ultimately calculated based on the actual substances participating in the conversion process. ### 2.6. This broad peak also overlaps with the N–H stretching vibrational peak, which is usually found about 3000–3400 cm⁻¹ for systems containing urea (AlOmar et al., 2016). The C=O stretching vibrational peak of all carboxylic acid-based DES exhibited a significant shift (e.g., from 1683 to 1716 cm⁻¹ in the oxalic acid system), indicating a disruption of the acid dimer structure (Fig. 2B-D). The peak positions and shapes of the O–H bands in alcohol-based DES were modified, further confirming the reorganisation of the hydrogen bonding network (Fig. 2E-F) (Jiang et al., 2020). The most significant alteration was observed in the ChCl/Urea system, where the N–H peak of urea exhibited a notable redshift and broadening, resulting in its merging with the O–H peak of ChCl to create a single broad peak (Fig. 2G). Additionally, the C=O peak also experienced a redshift. The significant redshift of the N–H peak indicates that the Cl⁻ ion in ChCl facilitates a strong hydrogen bonding interaction with the N–H group in urea, leading to the establishment of an N–H–Cl⁻ bond, which is crucial for the formation of deep eutectic solvents (Ashworth et al., 2016). At a temperature of 150 °C, the viscosity of all DES significantly decreases, with DES1 and DES2 exhibiting the most pronounced reductions, achieving viscosities of 52.2 mPa·s and 23.0 mPa·s, respectively. This observation is consis- tent with the Arrhenius equation, which suggests that increased tem- peratures diminish intermolecular hydrogen bond interactions, consequently improving molecular mobility. As shown in Table 1, carboxylic acid-based DES (DES1-DES3) exhibit higher α values than alcohol-based and amide-based DES, reflecting stronger hydrogen bond acidity due to the presence of organic acids (Zhang et al., 2023). DES1 shows the highest α value (2.53), correlating with its lowest pH, indicating oxalic acid's stronger acidity compared to citric and lactic acids. ChCl/alcohol DES had higher β-values than ChCl/carboxylic acid DES, which is consistent with previous studies (Zhang et al., 2023). In general, the β-value of DES is correlated with the length of the alkyl chain of the polyol (Zhang et al., 2023). Among them, DES5 has the highest β value, which may be due to the fact that 1,4-butanediol has the longest alkyl chain.The π* parameter highlights that higher values indicate stronger polarity, with ChCl-acid DES exhibiting π* values around 1.10, in line with previous findings (Zhang et al., 2023). This is due to low pH environments favoring protonation reactions, which activate methyl-oxygen bonds and accelerate demethylation. In addition, previous studies have indi- cated that the ChCl/CA system can form more hydrogen bonds with solutes, with an increased hydrogen bond lifetime compared to other solvents (Huang et al., 2024). Furthermore, DES viscosity demonstrated a perfect positive correlation with CE (r = 0.87, p = 2.4e-06). The strength of hydrogen bonding in DESs is positively correlated with their viscosity. Our findings show that ChCl/OA and ChCl/CA exhibit higher viscosities than other DESs, implying a greater number of hydrogen bonds, which may enhance interactions with PMFs (Table 1). Effect of Microwave Power As shown in Fig. 5C, the conversion efficiency follows a trend of initially increasing and then decreasing with changes in microwave power. At 160 W, the conversion efficiency reaches its minimum value (80.01 ± 0.88 %). Increasing the power to 480 W results in the highest conversion efficiency (90.47 ± 0.74 %, p < 0.05). Therefore, while a certain level of microwave power is necessary to overcome the activation energy for the demethylation reaction, excessive power appears to be detrimental, causing compound degradation that outweighs the increase in conversion rate. Comparison with other methods To date, various methods have been developed to hydroxylate PMFs into 5-OH-PMFs (Table 2). This study presents a novel microwave-assisted conversion system based on a deep eutectic solvent composed of choline chloride and citric acid (ChCl/CA). By optimizing process parameters, this method achieves significantly enhanced conversion efficiency. Compared with existing methods, this approach offers notable advantages, including environmental sustainability, high efficiency, and operational simplicity. Traditional conversion methods employing boron tribromide (BBr3) achieve high conversion efficiency but require toxic reagents and must be conducted under stringent conditions, such as low temperatures and the use of high-purity solvents. Additionally, these methods generate substantial quantities of hazardous byproducts during post-reaction processing, posing environmental and safety concerns (Li et al., 2007). The conversion method based on heating with hydrochloric acid, while requiring less specialized equipment, involves a prolonged reaction time of up to 24 h. Moreover, the corrosive and volatile nature of hydro- chloric acid creates operational safety risks, which limit its feasibility for industrial applications (XU et al., 2015). In recent years, edible acid-phosphoric acid systems have gained attention due to their higher safety profile. However, such systems require a reaction time of 2 h and achieve a conversion rate of approximately 93%, leaving room for improvement in both efficiency and product purification (Huang et al., 2019). The ChCl/CA DES system proposed in this study addresses many of the limitations associated with traditional methods. It eliminates the need for toxic reagents, significantly reduces reaction time, and operates under milder and safer conditions. Specifically, the hydroxyl group at the C5-position plays a pivotal role. 5-OH group forms a strong intramolecular hydrogen bond with the adjacent carbonyl oxygen at the C4-position (Li et al., 2006). This intramolecular hydrogen bond not only stabilizes the parent molecule but, more importantly, stabilizes the phenoxyl radical formed after hydrogen donation. This stabilization effect lowers the bond dissociation energy of the 5-OH group, making it a more efficient hydrogen donor and thus enhancing the molecule's overall ability to scavenge free radicals and terminate oxidative chain reactions. These findings highlight the potential of 5-OH-PMFs as potent antioxidants, offering promising applications in functional foods or as therapeutic agents for oxidative stress-related diseases. ### 3.6.2. Anti-inflammatory activity of 5-OH-PMFs The anti-inflammatory activity of PMFs and 5-OH-PMFs were evaluated in a LPS-induced inflammatory model in RAW264.7 cells. As shown in Fig. 7D, both PMFs and 5-OH-PMFs inhibited nitric oxide (NO) production in a concentration-dependent manner. Notably, 5-OH-PMFs exhibited significantly higher efficacy, reducing NO levels were reduced to near baseline levels at a concentration of 20 µg/mL. In terms of cytokine regulation, 5-OH-PMFs exhibited superior activity compared to PMFs. Specifically, 5-OH-PMFs significantly upregulated the expression of anti-inflammatory cytokines (such as TGF-β and IL-10) while effectively suppressing the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (such as IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α). These results highlight the potential of 5-OH-PMFs as a more potent anti-inflammatory agent than PMFs. Their ability to regulate inflammatory mediators and restore cytokine balance makes them a promising candidate for therapeutic strategies in the management of inflammatory diseases. 3.6.3. In vitro digestion of 5-OH-PMFs A three-stage in vitro digestion model (oral-gastric-intestinal) was employed to investigate the solubility changes of 5-OH-PMFs and PMFs throughout different stages of digestion. As depicted in Fig. 7E, the solubility of all tested compounds increased to varying extents following simulated gastrointestinal digestion. Among the three stages, intestinal digestion exerted the most pronounced solubilization effect, followed by gastric digestion, while oral digestion had a comparatively minor impact. Specifically, the solubility of 5-DN prior to digestion was 1.27 ± 0.09%, which increased to 1.67 ± 0.02% after oral digestion, further rose to 2.99 ± 0.007% after gastric digestion, and significantly surged to 13.04 ± 0.16% following intestinal digestion. Conversely, the solu- bility of NOB during the respective digestion stages was 1.78 ± 0.04%, 1.89 ± 0.005%, 2.82 ± 0.01%, and 4.35 ± 0.05%. Remarkably, the solubility of 5-DN post-intestinal digestion was approximately three times greater than that of NOB (p < 0.05). Interestingly, the solubility of TAN was significantly higher than that of 5-DT across all stages of digestion (p < 0.05), which contrasted the trend observed in the 5-DN/ NOB comparison. These findings indicate that the influence of hydroxy substitution on solubility behavior is compound-specific. The findings demonstrate that the intestinal environment exerts the most pronounced promotive effect on the solubility of flavonoids, aligning with the established understanding that flavonoids are pre- dominantly absorbed in the intestine (Karn et al., 2021). The substantial increase in solubility observed during the intestinal digestion phase can likely be attributed to the solubilizing action of bile salts. These salts exhibit surfactant properties that facilitate the formation of micellar structures with hydrophobic flavonoids, thereby markedly enhancing their solubility in aqueous systems(Obeid et al., 2025). Furthermore, the distinct solubility profiles of 5-OH-PMFs and PMFs throughout digestion underscore the critical role of molecular structure in determining bioavailability. Typically, the hydroxyl group serves as a hydrogen bond donor, which strengthens interactions with polar solvents, thus potentially increasing solubility (Lee et al., 2023). However, 5-DT exhibits lower solubility compared to TAN, which may be attributed to its higher log P value (Supplementary Table S10). This increased lipophilicity is likely a result of hydrogen bonding interactions between the 5-hydroxy group and the adjacent carbonyl atom (Zhang et al., 2021). Elevated lipophilicity generally enhances a compound's intestinal membrane permeability, potentially contributing to increased biological activity in vivo. 4. Conclusion This study demonstrated that employing strong carboxylic acid-based DES for the demethylation modification of citrus PMFs represents a green and sustainable strategy for enhancing the biological activity of PMFs. The pH, hydrogen bond strength, Kamlet-Taft α, and π* parameters of DES were identified as the key factors influencing PMF demethylation. Based on this, a green method was developed using a microwave-assisted choline chloride-citric acid (ChCl/CA) deep eutectic solvent system to catalyze citrus PMFs for the production of 5-OH-PMFs (primarily 5-DN and 5-DT). The optimal conversion efficiency of PMFs under this system reached 96.32 ± 0.06%. Compared with traditional methods, this system significantly shortened the reaction time, demonstrating higher reaction efficiency and resource utilization. Additionally, 5-OH-PMFs exhibited markedly enhanced antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities compared to their parent compounds, highlighting their potential applications in health-related products. However, the high viscosity of the DES system presents a challenge for operational simplicity. Fortunately, this limitation can potentially be mitigated through further optimization of the DES formulation. Additionally, the transformative mechanism of DES in the hydroxylation of PMFs warrants further investigation, which could provide valuable theoretical insights for designing customized DES formulations tailored to the preparation of natural bioactive compounds. In summary, this study provides a promising technical approach for the efficient preparation of 5-OH-PMFs and lays a solid foundation for their future development and application in bioactive product innovation. Demethylation modification plays an important role in enhancing the biological activity of natural products. Recent studies have revealed the potential of DES to promote demethylation reactions during ligno-cellulose processing. For instance, studies indicate that during the stepwise separation and depolymerisation of lignin by acidic DES, the demethylation of lignin structural units occurs concurrently with the cleavage of β-O-4' ether bonds (Hong et al., 2020). However, thoses studies mainly focus on the overall conversion of biopolymeric macro-molecules such as lignin, with no systematic investigation into deme-thylation reactions within specific bioactive compounds (Hong et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2025). It is unclear whether DESs can serve as efficient green catalysts for the selective demethylation of small-molecule bioactive substances. Inspired by the demethylation phenomena observed in lignin studies, we hypothesise that DES may offer an inno-vative and effective strategy for the controlled demethylation of bioac-tive molecules. Polymethoxyflavones (PMFs) are characteristic secondary metabo- lites produced by citrus plants, exhibiting bioactivities such as antioxi- dant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer, and lipid metabolism regulation (Peng et al., 2022). However, the primary active forms of PMFs that exert their effects in vivo are their demethylated products. These demethylated PMFs exhibit significantly enhanced bioavailability compared to their original forms (Ho et al., 2020). This makes the demethylation of PMFs a key pathway for enhancing the functional value of citrus resources. Several studies have explored various ap- proaches to convert PMFs to 5-OH-PMFs, including acid hydrolysis (Li et al., 2007), thermal treatment (Zhang et al., 2019a, 2019b) and mi- crobial biotransformation (Łużny et al., 2021). Among these, Brønsted acid-based hydrolysis has emerged as the main method for producing 5-OH-PMFs (Huang et al., 2019). The reaction mechanism likely due to the following: (1) existence of lone pairs of oxygen atoms in the methoxy group of PMFs and the oxygen atom of the adjacent carbonyl group, which are prone to proton activation; (2) presence of acidic solution providing protons; (3) the proton hydrogen and electron donating ox- ygen coordination to form a stable six-membered ring structure; (4) the broken covalent bond between the oxygen atom and methyl group; (5) hydrolysis of the six-membered ring to form a hydroxyl group (Huang et al., 2019). However, liquid acids are difficult to recover, corrode equipment, and pollute the environment. Although heating is safer, it is inefficient and offers low product selectivity. Microbial conversion re- quires complex equipment and similarly exhibits poor selectivity. These limitations hinder the realization of green production goals. Various physical techniques are also extensively used to enhance demethylation. High-temperature treatment significantly increases re- action rates. For instance, phosphoric acid-catalysed demethylation of naringin achieves 93.71% conversion within two hours at 175 °C (Huang et al., 2019). Hot pressurised water technology enhances acid-catalysed demethylation by altering water's physicochemical properties (Bocus et al., 2025). Ultrasound-assisted technology (UAE) uses locally generated high temperatures and pressures via cavitation effects to disrupt plant cell walls and enhance mass transfer (Sun et al., 2020). Microwave-assisted technology (MAE) selectively heats polar molecules, inducing intense molecular motion and friction to accelerate chemical reactions (Zhang et al., 2025). These studies demonstrate that integrating physical enhancement techniques with DES holds considerable potential, offering diverse intensification approaches for PMF demethylation. This study investigated the effects of DES type (carboxylic acid, alcohol and amide-based), physicochemical properties (pH, hydrogen bond strength, Kamlet-Taft parameter), and physical techniques (mi- crowave, high temperature and pressure, ultrasound-bath) on the demethylation of PMFs. Based on this, key reaction parameters were optimized, including microwave power, reaction time, DES water con- tent, and feed-to-liquid ratio. Additionally, the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities of 5-OH-PMFs were evaluated. The results of this study indicate that acidic DES have potential in the preparation of hy- droxylated PMFs extracts and other demethylated bioactive compounds. ## 2. Methods ### 2.1. A very strong negative correlation was observed between pH and CE (r = -0.74, p = 5e-04), indicating that acidic conditions significantly enhance the demethylation reaction. This is due to low pH environments favoring protonation reactions, which activate methyl-oxygen bonds and accelerate demethylation. In addition, previous studies have indi- cated that the ChCl/CA system can form more hydrogen bonds with solutes, with an increased hydrogen bond lifetime compared to other solvents (Huang et al., 2024). Our findings show that ChCl/OA and ChCl/CA exhibit higher viscosities than other DESs, implying a greater number of hydrogen bonds, which may enhance interactions with PMFs (Table 1). Effect of Microwave Power As shown in Fig. 5C, the conversion efficiency follows a trend of initially increasing and then decreasing with changes in microwave power. At 160 W, the conversion efficiency reaches its minimum value (80.01 ± 0.88 %). Increasing the power to 480 W results in the highest conversion efficiency (90.47 ± 0.74 %, p < 0.05). High microwave power can generate intense localized 'hot spots' within the reaction system, leading to rapid and potentially uncontrolled temperature increases. Flavonoids, including PMFs, are known to be thermally sensitive (Huang et al., 2019). Therefore, while a certain level of microwave power is necessary to overcome the activation energy for the demethylation reaction, excessive power appears to be detrimental, causing compound degradation that outweighs the increase in conversion rate. Comparison with other methods To date, various methods have been developed to hydroxylate PMFs into 5-OH-PMFs (Table 2). This study presents a novel microwave-assisted conversion system based on a deep eutectic solvent composed of choline chloride and citric acid (ChCl/CA). By optimizing process parameters, this method achieves significantly enhanced conversion efficiency. Compared with existing methods, this approach offers notable advantages, including environmental sustainability, high efficiency, and operational simplicity. Traditional conversion methods employing boron tribromide (BBr3) achieve high conversion efficiency but require toxic reagents and must be conducted under stringent conditions, such as low temperatures and the use of high-purity solvents. Additionally, these methods generate substantial quantities of hazardous byproducts during post-reaction processing, posing environmental and safety concerns (Li et al., 2007). The conversion method based on heating with hydrochloric acid, while requiring less specialized equipment, involves a prolonged reaction time of up to 24 h. Moreover, the corrosive and volatile nature of hydro- chloric acid creates operational safety risks, which limit its feasibility for industrial applications (XU et al., 2015). In recent years, edible acid-phosphoric acid systems have gained attention due to their higher safety profile. However, such systems require a reaction time of 2 h and achieve a conversion rate of approximately 93%, leaving room for improvement in both efficiency and product purification (Huang et al., 2019). The ChCl/CA DES system proposed in this study addresses many of the limitations associated with traditional methods. It eliminates the need for toxic reagents, significantly reduces reaction time, and operates under milder and safer conditions. As depicted in Fig. 7E, the solubility of all tested compounds increased to varying extents following simulated gastrointestinal digestion. Among the three stages, intestinal digestion exerted the most pronounced solubilization effect, followed by gastric digestion, while oral digestion had a comparatively minor impact. Specifically, the solubility of 5-DN prior to digestion was 1.27 ± 0.09%, which increased to 1.67 ± 0.02% after oral digestion, further rose to 2.99 ± 0.007% after gastric digestion, and significantly surged to 13.04 ± 0.16% following intestinal digestion. Remarkably, the solubility of 5-DN post-intestinal digestion was approximately three times greater than that of NOB (p < 0.05). Interestingly, the solubility of TAN was significantly higher than that of 5-DT across all stages of digestion (p < 0.05), which contrasted the trend observed in the 5-DN/ NOB comparison. These findings indicate that the influence of hydroxy substitution on solubility behavior is compound-specific. The findings demonstrate that the intestinal environment exerts the most pronounced promotive effect on the solubility of flavonoids, aligning with the established understanding that flavonoids are pre- dominantly absorbed in the intestine (Karn et al., 2021). The substantial increase in solubility observed during the intestinal digestion phase can likely be attributed to the solubilizing action of bile salts. These salts exhibit surfactant properties that facilitate the formation of micellar structures with hydrophobic flavonoids, thereby markedly enhancing their solubility in aqueous systems(Obeid et al., 2025). Furthermore, the distinct solubility profiles of 5-OH-PMFs and PMFs throughout digestion underscore the critical role of molecular structure in determining bioavailability. Typically, the hydroxyl group serves as a hydrogen bond donor, which strengthens interactions with polar solvents, thus potentially increasing solubility (Lee et al., 2023). However, 5-DT exhibits lower solubility compared to TAN, which may be attributed to its higher log P value (Supplementary Table S10). This increased lipophilicity is likely a result of hydrogen bonding interactions between the 5-hydroxy group and the adjacent carbonyl atom (Zhang et al., 2021). Elevated lipophilicity generally enhances a compound's intestinal membrane permeability, potentially contributing to increased biological activity in vivo. 4. Conclusion This study demonstrated that employing strong carboxylic acid-based DES for the demethylation modification of citrus PMFs represents a green and sustainable strategy for enhancing the biological activity of PMFs. The pH, hydrogen bond strength, Kamlet-Taft α, and π* parameters of DES were identified as the key factors influencing PMF demethylation. Based on this, a green method was developed using a microwave-assisted choline chloride-citric acid (ChCl/CA) deep eutectic solvent system to catalyze citrus PMFs for the production of 5-OH-PMFs (primarily 5-DN and 5-DT). The optimal conversion efficiency of PMFs under this system reached 96.32 ± 0.06%. Compared with traditional methods, this system significantly shortened the reaction time, demonstrating higher reaction efficiency and resource utilization. Additionally, 5-OH-PMFs exhibited markedly enhanced antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities compared to their parent compounds, highlighting their potential applications in health-related products. However, the high viscosity of the DES system presents a challenge for operational simplicity. Fortunately, this limitation can potentially be mitigated through further optimization of the DES formulation. Additionally, the transformative mechanism of DES in the hydroxylation of PMFs warrants further investigation, which could provide valuable theoretical insights for designing customized DES formulations tailored to the preparation of natural bioactive compounds. In summary, this study provides a promising technical approach for the efficient preparation of 5-OH-PMFs and lays a solid foundation for their future development and application in bioactive product innovation.
